planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into well-drained, sandy to average soil; this fast-rooting groundcover knits together quickly wherever a trailing stem touches soil, so a few starter plugs fill in within a season.

directions: Grow in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun to partial shade; pink-headed knotweed forms a fast, dense, ankle-high mat of small oval leaves marked with a dark maroon chevron, studded from spring through the first hard frost with tiny clover-like pink flower heads on wiry pink-tinged stems. It roots wherever a trailing stem touches soil, which makes it an efficient bare-slope or path-edge filler but also means it spreads readily and should be sited with a hard edge (paving, a mow strip) to keep it in bounds, since it self-sows and naturalizes aggressively in mild climates and is considered invasive in parts of the West Coast. In zones at the cold edge of its range it dies to the ground each winter and returns from surviving crowns or self-sown seedlings, effectively behaving as a reseeding annual. Shear back hard in early spring to remove winter-damaged growth before new shoots emerge.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Blackfield Mountain Fleece (Near-Black Bud Red Bistort)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into moist, fertile soil; 'Blackfield' forms a full, bushy clump by its second season and does not need staking even at mature size.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; 'Blackfield' opens its tightly packed flower spikes from buds so dark they read almost black, unfurling into an intense, saturated blood-red as the wands mature, a color combination that gives the clump a smoldering two-tone look through its long midsummer-to-fall bloom season. The bushy, compact habit stays tidier and more self-supporting than the taller mountain fleece selections, making it easier to place mid-border without props. Pollinators work the spikes steadily once they open. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep flowering vigorous and renew the deepest bud color.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into moist to wet, moderately fertile soil; give 'Alba' full sun for the heaviest bloom, with light afternoon shade appreciated in hot, humid summer climates.

directions: Grow in average, medium-to-wet soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Alba' carries slender, densely packed spires of small white, bell-shaped flowers on tall wands held well above a mound of oval, pointed, mid-green leaves, blooming from midsummer into fall. The clean white color reads brightly against the dark foliage of neighboring shade perennials and makes a useful cooling contrast next to the many red and pink mountain fleece cultivars. Best flower production comes in full sun, but the plant tolerates and often appreciates part shade in hot climates where afternoon sun can scorch the foliage. Divide crowded clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts in spring into moist, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed; this clump-forming selection is grown for its foliage and spreads slowly compared with seed-grown Persicaria species.

directions: Grow in full sun to partial shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil; 'Silver Dragon' is a foliage selection whose triangular leaves are heavily brushed with metallic silver-gray over a green base, with a darker chevron marking near the leaf center that deepens the contrast. Wiry red-tinged stems carry small white flower spikes in late summer, but as with 'Red Dragon' the leaf color is the main ornamental draw, and the bright, reflective foliage lights up shadier corners of the garden more effectively than plain green-leaved Persicaria. Where marginally hardy it can be treated as a striking annual foliage plant, and elsewhere it dies back to the crown each winter and re-emerges reliably in spring. Cut back the previous year's dried stems in late winter before new growth begins.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Darjeeling Red' spreads by rhizomes to form a dense, low mat and tolerates dry shade under trees once established.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of Himalayan fleeceflower opens deeper rose-red flower spikes than the species from midsummer into fall, aging to a rich russet as the season progresses so older and newer spikes bloom together in a two-tone display. The dense, semi-evergreen mat of lance-shaped leaves takes on strong bronze-red fall color and persists through mild winters. It spreads at a steady, moderate pace by rhizomes and tolerates dry shade under established trees better than most flowering groundcovers once established. Cut back old flower spikes and tidy foliage in late winter before new growth begins.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; give this vigorous species room to spread and stake or grow it through supportive neighbors, since its tall stems can flop when the plant is in full flower.

directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Armenian cranesbill is a big, sprawling species prized for its large, cup-shaped, magenta-crimson flowers with a near-black center and dark veining radiating out across each petal, produced in profusion over a long midsummer season. The heart-shaped leaves are handsomely cut and color crimson-red in fall, adding a second season of interest after bloom. It tolerates part shade well, though flowering is heaviest in full sun, and its size and vigor make it a striking presence weaving through or behind smaller perennials. Cut the entire clump back hard after the first flush to control its sprawling habit and often coax a smaller repeat bloom later in the season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in average, dry-to-medium, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; Caucasian cranesbill is a compact, mounding species suited to the front of a border, rock garden, or wall crevice.

directions: Plant in average, dry-to-medium, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Caucasian cranesbill forms a tidy, low mound of sage-green, velvety, finely wrinkled, lobed leaves that stay attractive all season even without flowers, and in late spring to early summer carries pale white to soft lavender-white blooms delicately veined in violet just above the foliage. It is notably drought-tolerant once established and shrugs off hot, humid summers better than many hardy geraniums, making it a good choice for lean, well-drained sites where richer soil would cause floppier growth. Trim lightly after bloom to keep the mound compact; otherwise it needs almost no maintenance.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; this naturally occurring dwarf variety stays lower and denser than the straight species, spreading gradually into a trailing mat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade; this dwarf, trailing form of blood-red cranesbill (long sold under the name 'Lancastriense') carries pale pink flowers finely penciled with dark red veins over a low, dense mound of finely cut foliage, staying noticeably shorter and more compact than the magenta-flowered species. Like its parent it is exceptionally drought- and lime-tolerant, thriving in rocky banks, wall crevices, and gravelly soil where richer, moister ground would cause looser, less floriferous growth. A light shearing after the main early-summer bloom keeps the mat tidy and can prompt a modest repeat flush. Long-lived and essentially maintenance-free once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; 'Samobor' is grown as much for its marked foliage as its flowers, so give it a visible spot along a shaded path or border edge.

directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Samobor' pairs the small, dark, reflexed-petaled, deep maroon flowers typical of mourning widow with broad, lobed leaves boldly stamped with a chocolate-purple crescent near the center of each leaflet, so the foliage reads as an ornamental feature from the moment it emerges in spring, well before bloom. Like the species it is among the most shade-tolerant geraniums available, performing well even in the dense dry shade cast by mature evergreens. Cut the clump back by half after flowering to refresh the leaf marking and prompt a tidy new flush of foliage for the rest of the season. Self-sows modestly to naturalize in shaded woodland settings.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the surface of moist mix 6-8 weeks before last frost, as light aids germination; plants form a basal rosette the first year and bloom from the second year on, behaving as a short-lived true perennial rather than a biennial.

directions: Plant in reasonably dry, well-drained soil in full sun; chocolate foxglove is a true perennial species from Spain and Portugal, distinct from the biennial common foxglove, that produces narrow, densely packed spires tightly set with small chocolate-brown flowers netted in violet veining and finished with a darker mahogany lower lip. The gray-green, lance-shaped leaves form a low rosette that stays evergreen in mild winters. Unlike common foxglove it prefers a lean, sharply drained site and resents wet, heavy soil, especially over winter. All parts are highly toxic if ingested and should be handled with gloves. Cut back spent spikes to tidy the clump, and expect it to persist and slowly bulk up for several years where its drainage needs are met.

common_name: Snow Thimble Foxglove (First-Year-Blooming Pure White Foxglove)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors in late summer for fall transplanting where foxglove is grown as a winter annual or biennial, or sow in very early spring under lights 10-12 weeks before the last frost for first-year bloom farther north; 'Snow Thimble' was bred to flower reliably in its first year from an early sowing.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil. 'Snow Thimble' produces tall, architectural spires densely set with pure white, outward-facing bells with a lightly textured throat and none of the maroon speckling found in most foxglove strains, giving it a cleaner, more luminous look in the garden and as a cut flower. Blooming from an early sowing the first year rather than requiring the traditional two-year biennial wait, it fits more easily into an annually refreshed border. Provide afternoon shade in hot climates and keep soil consistently moist but never soggy. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas frequented by children or pets and wear gloves when handling the foliage.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Digitalis purpurea as a Southern Biennial

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring into moist, well-drained soil; 'Goldcrest' is a sterile hybrid propagated only by division or cuttings, never by seed, so purchase nursery-grown plants rather than looking for seed.

directions: Plant in moist but well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Goldcrest' is a compact hybrid between Digitalis obscura and Digitalis grandiflora with smooth, semi-evergreen, lance-shaped leaves quite unlike the fuzzy, wide foliage of common foxglove hybrids. Sterile and unable to set seed, it channels all its energy into flowering continuously from midsummer into early fall rather than setting one flush of spikes and going to seed, producing upright racemes of warm peachy-yellow, trumpet-shaped blooms lightly marked in reddish brown in the throat. Its shorter, sturdier, clump-forming habit needs no staking and suits the middle of a border better than taller purpurea-type foxgloves. Deadheading is unnecessary, but shearing spent spikes tidies the clump and can prompt a fresh flush.
